extracted.intended_audience: students of differential equations / dynamical systems (advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and criteria for classifying equilibria (stable, asymptotically stable, unstable, saddles), using linearization, Lyapunov functions, nullclines, and recognizing basic bifurcations (saddle-node, pitchfork, Hopf, heteroclinic). Emphasis on planar systems and some higher-dimensional remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable equilibrium (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: X* is a stable equilibrium if for every neighborhood O of X* in R^n there is a neighborhood O1 of X* in O such that every solution X(t) with X(0)=X0 in O1 is defined and remains in O for all t>0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical interpretation: nearby solutions stay nearby for all future time; stability is required for physical relevance because positions can only be approximated. This is the precise topological (Lyapunov) notion of stability; used as a baseline when judging an equilibrium's physical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymptotic stability (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: X* is asymptotically stable if it is stable and, in addition, there exists O1 such that every solution starting in O1 satisfies lim_{t→∞} X(t) = X*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asymptotically stable equilibria are 'visible' in applications since nearby solutions not only stay near but converge to the equilibrium. Often the most important type of equilibrium in applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unstable equilibrium (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An equilibrium X* that is not stable is called unstable: there is a neighborhood O of X* such that for every neighborhood O1 of X* in O there is at least one solution X(t) starting at X(0)∈O1 which does not lie entirely in O for all t>0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instability means some arbitrarily small perturbations lead solutions to leave any prescribed neighborhood; examples include sources and saddles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearization criterion for asymptotic stability (hyperbolic sink)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the n-dimensional system X' = F(X) has an equilibrium point at X* and all of the eigenvalues of the linearized system at X* have negative real parts, then X* is asymptotically stable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the equilibrium is hyperbolic (no eigenvalues with zero real part), the linearization immediately determines stability. This gives a straightforward test: compute Jacobian at X* and check eigenvalues' real parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonhyperbolic limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: When the linearization of the system at an equilibrium point is nonhyperbolic (has eigenvalues with zero real part), stability cannot be decided universally by linearization alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases one must use other techniques (e.g., Lyapunov functions, normal form / center manifold methods, or find solutions). There is no universal method that works in all nonhyperbolic cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local stable/unstable manifolds for higher-dimensional saddles
rubrics_metrics.description: If the linearized system at X0 has k eigenvalues with negative real parts and n−k eigenvalues with positive real parts, then the local stable and unstable sets are submanifolds of dimension k and n−k respectively. Locally the stable set is the graph of a C^∞ function g: B_r → R^{n−k} with g(0)=0 and all partial derivatives of g vanish at the origin; similarly for the unstable set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes the geometric nature of saddles in higher dimensions: stable/unstable manifolds are tangent at X0 to the corresponding eigenspaces and meet only at X0. Useful for understanding local phase structure without full manifold theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nullcline method (planar systems)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a planar system x' = f(x,y), y' = g(x,y), the x-nullcline is the set where x' = 0 (f=0) and the y-nullcline is where y' = 0 (g=0). Their intersections are equilibrium points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nullclines divide the plane into basic regions in which vector-field components have fixed signs; by sampling one point per basic region one determines the vector-field direction (NE, NW, SE, SW) throughout the region. This often suffices to sketch the qualitative phase portrait and deduce long-term behavior (e.g., which regions lead to infinity or to equilibria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using nullclines to detect invariant lines and global behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Nullclines can reveal invariant curves (e.g., when the vector field is tangent to a nullcline) and can be used to find saddle connections and global changes in flow (heteroclinic behavior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example guidance: if the vector field is tangent along x=±1 and y'=... has sign structure, one can see whether solutions approach along straight lines, whether heteroclinic connections exist, and how parameter changes move or break such connections (leading to bifurcations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heteroclinic connection and bifurcation signal
rubrics_metrics.description: A heteroclinic solution (saddle connection) is a solution that connects one saddle equilibrium to another (a branch of the unstable curve of one matching a branch of the stable curve of the other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such connections are atypical (fragile); when present they can be broken by small parameter changes and typically indicate a nearby bifurcation (a heteroclinic bifurcation) with significant global consequences (e.g., opening pathways between regions previously separated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Saddle-node bifurcation (qualitative description)
rubrics_metrics.description: A saddle-node bifurcation is a parameter value at which the number of equilibrium solutions changes: typically two equilibria in I if a<a0, one equilibrium if a=a0, and no equilibria if a>a0 (or reversed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saddle-node bifurcations often occur when the linearization has a zero eigenvalue. The bifurcation diagram plots equilibria versus the parameter and shows the birth/annihilation of a saddle and a node (or sink/source).

rubrics_metrics.name: Saddle-node bifurcation (technical conditions for first-order)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose x' = f_a(x) and at (x0,a0) one has f_{a0}(x0)=0 and f'_ {a0}(x0)=0. If additionally f''_{a0}(x0) != 0 and (∂f_a/∂a)_{(x0,a0)} != 0, then the differential equation undergoes a saddle-node bifurcation at a=a0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the usual nondegeneracy and transversality conditions used to apply the implicit function theorem and show the local concave/convex behavior of the equilibrium curve; they guarantee the typical two/one/none scenario nearby.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitchfork bifurcation (example behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: For x' = x^3 − a x, there is a pitchfork bifurcation: when a ≤ 0 the only equilibrium is x=0; when a>0 equilibria at x=0 and x=±√a appear (three equilibria).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pitchfork bifurcations typically arise in symmetric systems and involve a symmetric splitting of an equilibrium into multiple symmetric equilibria; check symmetry and higher-derivative conditions to identify this bifurcation type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hopf bifurcation (qualitative description)
rubrics_metrics.description: At a Hopf bifurcation the linearization at an equilibrium has a pair of pure imaginary eigenvalues (and no zero eigenvalues) as the parameter passes through a critical value; no new equilibria arise but a periodic solution is born at the equilibrium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical signature: linearization eigenvalues a ± i with a changing sign; converting to polar coordinates often reveals a birth of a limit cycle (stable or unstable depending on nonlinear terms). Use normal form/center manifold techniques to determine stability of the resulting periodic orbit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyapunov function method (Liapunov Stability Theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let L:O→R be differentiable on an open set O containing an equilibrium X*. If (a) L(X*)=0 and L(X)>0 for X≠X*, and (b) 1L ≤ 0 in O\{X*}, then X* is stable. If additionally (c) 1L < 0 in O\{X*}, then X* is asymptotically stable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A function satisfying (a) and (b) is a Lyapunov (Liapunov) function; if (c) holds it is a strict Lyapunov function. Lyapunov's theorem allows proving (asymptotic) stability without solving the system, and can give estimates of the basin of attraction by the region where the conditions hold. Finding Lyapunov functions is typically ad hoc and requires ingenuity or physical insight (e.g., use energy in mechanical systems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing quadratic Lyapunov functions (example guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Try L(x)=a x^2 + b y^2 + c z^2 with positive coefficients; compute 1L = DL(F(X)) and choose coefficients to make 1L ≤ 0 (or <0) in a region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique is useful for polynomial/vector-field examples: choosing weights can cancel cross-terms and force nonpositivity. The textbook example shows setting a=1,b=2,c=1 to obtain 1L ≤ 0 and deduce stability or asymptotic stability depending on parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy as Lyapunov function (pendulum example)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the pendulum with friction parameter b≥0, the total energy E(θ,v)=1/2 v^2 + 1−cos θ satisfies 1E = −b v^2 ≤ 0, so E is a Lyapunov function and the downward rest is stable (strictly asymptotically stable if b>0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical or electrical energy often supplies natural Lyapunov functions. If 1E ≡ 0 (no damping), level sets of energy describe invariant curves and fully determine the phase portrait without solving ODEs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using nullclines and direction fields to deduce global phase portrait
rubrics_metrics.description: By labeling basic regions between nullclines and testing vector-field directions at representative points, one can determine flows: which regions are invariant, which solutions go to infinity, which approach equilibria, and the global arrangement of stable/unstable manifolds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: determine regions where vector field points into a region (so solutions remain and tend to infinity in a given direction), or locate unique stable curves separating basins of attraction. Nullcline sketches plus eigenvalue checks at equilibria often suffice for qualitative portraits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex vector field criterion (exploration hint)
rubrics_metrics.description: For complex ODE z' = F(z) with polynomial F, the complex derivative F'(z0) exists and equals the limit along any curve; writing F(x+iy)=u+iv and taking limits horizontally and vertically shows the Cauchy–Riemann equations must hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This observation lets one relate complex differentiability to planar vector-field structure and classify equilibrium types for complex polynomial vector fields. (Presented as an exploration with exercises.)
